paragraphs: FedLEASE addresses a problem in adapting language models when training data is spread across organizations with different needs. Federated learning supports collaboration across those clients, while LoRA makes adaptation less computationally demanding. However, the paper argues that a single LoRA module can struggle when clients represent substantially different domains. The challenge is deciding both which specialized modules to train and which ones each client should use.

The framework handles allocation by grouping clients according to similarities in their representations. These groups guide the allocation and training of domain-specific LoRA experts. It then uses an adaptive top-M mixture-of-experts mechanism so that individual clients can select how many experts to use. Allocation and selection therefore respond to different aspects of the problem: shared domain structure across clients and the particular needs of each client.

Experiments across diverse benchmark datasets report significant improvements over existing federated fine-tuning approaches in heterogeneous settings while maintaining communication efficiency. The findings support adapting the organization and use of lightweight experts to differences among participating clients.
neurips-2025-adaptive-lora-experts-alloc.tldr: FedLEASE groups similar clients and adapts their use of LoRA experts to improve federated fine-tuning on heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: AdaReasoner tackles the mismatch between fixed language-model configurations and tasks that demand different kinds of thinking. Settings such as temperature and reasoning steps may suit one task better than another, yet prompting methods often reuse a general configuration. The paper proposes a plugin that automatically chooses reasoning configurations, with the aim of making these choices responsive to the task.

The plugin learns through reinforcement learning. Its training combines a factorized action space, which separates configuration choices into components, with targeted exploration and a pretrained reward model. A few-shot guide helps direct the process. This makes configuration selection something a policy learns to perform, rather than a fixed collection of settings applied across all requests. The authors design the plugin to work independently of a particular underlying LLM.

The paper reports theoretical guarantees and experiments supporting fast convergence and a sublinear policy gap. Across six LLMs and varied reasoning tasks, AdaReasoner consistently improves over standard baselines, preserves out-of-distribution robustness, and improves knowledge-intensive tasks through tailored prompts. These findings support task-sensitive configuration within the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-adareasoner-adaptive-reason.tldr: AdaReasoner learns task-specific reasoning configurations that improve performance across six evaluated language models.

paragraphs: AgMMU evaluates whether vision-language models can combine visual detail with agricultural expertise. Its evidence comes from 116,231 real exchanges between growers and USDA-authorized Cooperative Extension experts. An automated extraction and question-generation pipeline, followed by human verification, turns these exchanges into a benchmark and a development corpus. This connects evaluation to questions people actually ask about agricultural problems.

The benchmark contains 746 multiple-choice questions and 746 open-ended questions. Its companion corpus, AgBase, provides 57,079 multimodal facts covering insect and species identification, disease categorization, symptom description, and management instruction. Pairing evaluation with development data matters because researchers can both measure weaknesses and train models using knowledge from the same specialist domain.

Testing 12 leading models reveals substantial weaknesses in fine-grained perception and factual grounding, with open-source models trailing proprietary models. Fine-tuning on AgBase improves open-ended performance, with reported average gains reaching up to 11.6%. The results indicate that domain-specific training can narrow the observed gap and that strong general-purpose capabilities do not automatically supply detailed agricultural understanding.
neurips-2025-agmmu-a-comprehensive-agric.tldr: AgMMU uses expert-answered agricultural questions to expose vision-language model weaknesses and provides training data that helps narrow them.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a gradually weakening regularization term changes stochastic gradient descent. The setting is convex optimization with smooth objective functions on a separable real Hilbert space. The algorithm adds Tikhonov regularization whose strength tends to zero over time. This introduces a way to guide the optimization trajectory while ultimately targeting the original, unregularized problem.

The main theoretical result is strong convergence to the solution with the smallest norm, without imposing additional boundedness assumptions. This matters when the original problem admits multiple solutions: the method has a specified destination among them. The paper also quantifies convergence rates and examines how step sizes should interact with the speed at which regularization disappears.

The analysis identifies decaying regularization as a mechanism for stabilizing the learning dynamics while controlling solution selection. Numerical experiments on image reconstruction and inverse problems based on ordinary differential equations support the theoretical findings. The conclusions concern the stated convex, smooth setting, including applications where recovering an underlying quantity from observations can be ill-posed.
neurips-2025-controlling-the-flow-stabil.tldr: For convex smooth problems, vanishing Tikhonov regularization guides SGD toward the minimum-norm solution with quantified convergence rates.

paragraphs: MOCOBO studies how a small collection of solutions can collectively serve many objectives. Coverage means that every objective has at least one good solution somewhere in the collection. For example, a set of antibiotics might cover several pathogens even though no individual antibiotic treats all of them. The target is a collection with fewer members than there are objectives.

The paper develops a Bayesian optimization method for this coverage problem. Its acquisition function, inspired by expected improvement, guides the search toward useful additions or improvements to collective coverage. This changes what counts as a successful search result: the value lies in how the selected solutions work together across objectives, rather than in requiring each solution to balance every objective.

On high-dimensional tasks including peptide and molecular design, the smaller collections match or nearly match the coverage obtained by optimizing each objective separately. Peptides identified by the method also show high potency against drug-resistant pathogens in laboratory experiments. Those results support the approach's potential for drug discovery without establishing clinical effectiveness.
neurips-2025-covering-multiple-objective.tldr: MOCOBO searches for small collections of solutions that collectively cover many objectives, with promising peptide-design results.

paragraphs: CTSketch addresses learning systems in which neural networks feed their predictions into a discrete symbolic program. Training uses labels for the final combined output, so the neural components must learn from supervision that arrives after symbolic processing. The paper focuses on making this arrangement scale when the symbolic computation involves many inputs.

The method divides the symbolic program into smaller subprograms and represents each with a compact tensor sketch. It then combines those sketches with distributions over the neural predictions using simple tensor operations. This approximates the program's output distribution while preserving a compositional structure: summaries of smaller computations become building blocks for the larger computation. The authors also provide theoretical insight into the maximum approximation error.

Evaluations include established neurosymbolic benchmarks and tasks designed to test scalability. The reported neural predictors achieve high accuracy on tasks involving one thousand inputs despite receiving supervision only on the final output. The results show that approximating symbolic inference through compositional sketches can extend the practical scale of this learning setup.
neurips-2025-ctsketch-compositional-tens.tldr: CTSketch compresses symbolic subprograms into tensor sketches, enabling accurate neurosymbolic learning on evaluated tasks with one thousand inputs.

paragraphs: Astro-DSB applies diffusion Schrödinger bridge models to inverse prediction problems in giant molecular clouds, where the scientific context is star formation. The goal is to use observations to infer quantities associated with a dynamical astrophysical system. The proposed model adapts the bridge framework using a pairwise domain assumption tailored to these dynamics.

The authors study both how the model learns and how well it predicts, using physically simulated data and real observations from Taurus B213. They report improvements in interpretability, learning efficiency, and prediction performance compared with conventional astrostatistical methods and other machine-learning approaches. These comparisons connect the modeling choice to practical observational inference rather than evaluating it only as a generative technique.

A second finding concerns simulated conditions outside the training distribution. Probabilistic generative modeling improves over discriminative pixel-to-pixel prediction when initial conditions or dominant physical processes change. The authors interpret this as evidence of learning beyond pure data statistics. It motivates further physics-aware generative modeling, while the reported evidence remains tied to the astrophysical tasks and distribution shifts studied.
neurips-2025-dynamic-diffusion-schroding.tldr: Astro-DSB adapts diffusion bridges for astrophysical inverse prediction and improves performance on studied observations and simulation shifts.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a matrix can be recovered exactly from a small random sample of noisy entries. The underlying setting requires low rank, sufficiently spread-out singular vectors, and enough observations. For noisy data, bounded precision is also central to the exact-recovery discussion: the target entries have limited precision rather than arbitrary real-valued detail.

Earlier results controlled average reconstruction error or obtained entrywise guarantees under extra restrictions on singular values. Those restrictions included either a small condition number or large gaps between successive singular values. The paper removes the need for these additional spectral restrictions in its recovery result. Its main computational step is truncated singular value decomposition, giving the proposed algorithm a simple and efficient core.

The theoretical contribution is a new infinity-norm version of the Davis–Kahan perturbation theorem, proved using a combinatorial contour integration argument. Entrywise control matters because a small average error can still hide individual mistakes that obstruct exact recovery. The result strengthens the recovery analysis while retaining the basic structural and sampling setting described in the abstract.
neurips-2025-fast-exact-recovery-of-nois.tldr: An efficient matrix-recovery method removes extra singular-value restrictions from exact recovery in the noisy, bounded-precision setting.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how a decoder-only Transformer can identify graph structure when its input arrives as a sequence. It concentrates on substructure extraction: finding relevant patterns within a larger graph. The analysis also examines the role of the input query, connecting the structure being sought with the model's internal processing.

The authors introduce Induced Substructure Filtration, or ISF, as a perspective on how identification unfolds across Transformer layers. Empirical results and theoretical analysis support this account, and further examination of LLMs reveals consistent internal dynamics across layers. The contribution is therefore an explanation of the extraction process, alongside evidence that the process appears in the models studied.

Building on that perspective, the paper explores thinking in substructures as a way to extract more complex composite patterns efficiently. It demonstrates extraction from attributed graphs, including molecular graphs, where graph elements carry additional information. These findings help explain how sequence-based models can perform structural tasks and extend the investigation beyond graphs represented only by their connections.
neurips-2025-from-sequence-to-structure-.tldr: The paper develops and tests an account of how Transformer layers identify graph substructures from sequential inputs.

paragraphs: This paper examines a weakness in defenses that inspect fine-tuning or inference samples individually. Such pointwise checks try to recognize harmful content one sample at a time. The authors show how misuse can instead depend on relationships among apparently benign samples, making individual harmlessness insufficient for identifying the broader behavior.

The demonstrated attack class uses semantic or syntactic variation in benign outputs to carry dangerous knowledge covertly. Its training and inference samples can be collected from the model before fine-tuning and are individually benign and low-perplexity. The key issue is that the meaning carried by the overall arrangement is not captured by judging each sample independently.

Tests against the OpenAI fine-tuning API elicit answers to harmful multiple-choice questions. The attacks also evade an enhanced monitoring system that detects other fine-tuning attacks. These results establish limitations of the pointwise defensive approach studied, rather than showing that every form of defense must fail. The authors consequently direct attention toward multi-point defenses that can examine relationships across samples.
neurips-2025-fundamental-limitations-in-.tldr: Individually benign samples can support fine-tuning misuse, exposing fundamental limits of defenses that inspect samples in isolation.

paragraphs: INFEX studies decision-making when exploration is useful but too costly or impractical to perform continually. In linear bandits, an algorithm must choose actions while learning their rewards. Fully adaptive methods may explore at every step, whereas purely greedy choices can fail without strong contextual diversity. The paper investigates a middle ground with explicitly scheduled exploration.

The framework runs a chosen exploratory policy at selected times and predominantly takes greedy actions between them. It is modular, allowing an existing fully adaptive exploration method to serve as the underlying policy. This separates the choice of exploration strategy from the decision about how frequently to invoke it, making the schedule a central part of the method.

The theoretical guarantee is conditional: when exploration frequency exceeds a logarithmic threshold, INFEX matches the instance-dependent regret of standard provably efficient algorithms. Restricting expensive exploration computations to selected intervals can also improve efficiency. Experiments support the analysis and report state-of-the-art regret performance with runtime improvements. The result supports infrequent exploration under the stated frequency condition, rather than arbitrarily rare exploration.
neurips-2025-infrequent-exploration-in-l.tldr: INFEX combines scheduled exploration with mostly greedy actions, matching strong regret guarantees when exploration exceeds a logarithmic threshold.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approximate normalization approach for Transformers. It addresses training problems such as numerical instability, overfitting, and increasing variation in the residual stream. Strictly placing parameters and representations on a hypersphere can help training but adds costs. The authors seek similar practical benefits using simpler operations and less rigid constraints.

Their approach uses scalar multiplications motivated by the observation that high-dimensional random-vector norms concentrate tightly. For parameters, it constrains norms instead of enforcing strict normalization. These changes remove the need for weight decay and learning-rate warm-up in the proposed setup, without increasing the total number of normalization layers. The method therefore changes how magnitudes are controlled throughout training.

Transformer experiments report up to 40% faster convergence than GPT models with QK normalization, with 3% additional runtime cost. The distinction matters: convergence speed and per-run computational overhead are separate measurements. Scaling-law investigations also find that the method supports larger training batches while preserving the favorable scaling behavior of classic GPT architectures. These are reported benefits of the evaluated training approach.
neurips-2025-learning-in-compact-spaces-.tldr: Approximate normalization and parameter-norm constraints accelerate Transformer convergence in experiments with modest runtime overhead.

paragraphs: LT-Soups addresses classification datasets where some classes have many examples and others have very few. The paper finds that parameter-efficient adaptation methods can preserve performance on rare tail classes while sacrificing accuracy on common head classes. It identifies the proportion of head classes to tail classes as a crucial factor in this trade-off, alongside the severity of sample imbalance.

Controlled CIFAR100 experiments vary both factors. They show that parameter-efficient methods work particularly well in tail-heavy settings but degrade in more balanced or head-heavy distributions. LT-Soups responds with two stages: first, it averages models fine-tuned on balanced subsets to reduce head-class bias; then it fine-tunes only the classifier using the full dataset to restore head-class accuracy.

Across six benchmark datasets, the method achieves better head–tail trade-offs than parameter-efficient fine-tuning and traditional model soups over varied imbalance regimes. The findings make the dataset's class composition part of the adaptation decision. They also support separating the creation of less biased representations from the final adjustment of the classifier to the full training distribution.
neurips-2025-lt-soups-bridging-head-and-.tldr: LT-Soups averages models trained on balanced subsets, then adjusts the classifier to improve accuracy trade-offs between common and rare classes.

paragraphs: MeanFlow tackles generative modeling with a single model evaluation. The paper changes the quantity that the model learns about a flow: it uses average velocity over an interval, while Flow Matching methods model instantaneous velocity. This focuses training on movement across an interval, which is directly relevant when generation must happen in one step.

The authors derive an identity connecting average and instantaneous velocities and use it to guide neural-network training. The resulting method is self-contained: it does not require a pretrained model, distillation from another model, or curriculum learning. That matters because the reported one-step capability is learned directly rather than obtained through those additional training stages.

Trained from scratch on ImageNet at 256 × 256 resolution, MeanFlow achieves an FID of 3.43 with one function evaluation. The paper reports a substantial improvement over previous state-of-the-art one-step diffusion and flow models. It also reports a narrower performance gap with multistep models, supporting average velocity as a useful foundation for one-step generation without claiming that the gap has disappeared.
neurips-2025-mean-flows-for-one-step-gen.tldr: MeanFlow learns average flow velocity to generate images in one evaluation, achieving strong results when trained from scratch.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to develop preference-optimization algorithms without relying exclusively on expensive language-model alignment experiments. Such evaluations can be noisy and depend on model size and training settings. The authors build a diagnostic suite of MuJoCo tasks and preference datasets to create a cheaper, more controlled setting for comparing algorithms.

They then introduce Mirror Preference Optimization, a family of methods based on mirror descent. Evolutionary strategies search within this family for algorithms suited to particular dataset characteristics, including noisy preferences and mixtures of data quality. The search therefore adapts the optimization objective to the structure of the preference data, rather than assuming one existing objective is best across all settings.

The discovered methods outperform all known algorithms in the targeted MuJoCo settings, according to the paper. Insights from those experiments also guide the design of a new algorithm that significantly exceeds existing baselines on an LLM alignment task. This provides evidence that simpler diagnostic environments can yield useful alignment insights, while the demonstrated transfer concerns the particular language-model task evaluated.
neurips-2025-meta-learning-objectives-fo.tldr: The paper searches for preference-optimization objectives in cheaper MuJoCo tasks and transfers the resulting insights to improve an LLM alignment task.

paragraphs: MiniMax-Remover targets video object removal, where unwanted objects must disappear without introducing replacement objects or visual artifacts. Existing diffusion-based approaches can also require costly sampling and classifier-free guidance. The paper proposes a two-stage method that simplifies the underlying model and then trains it to withstand noise patterns associated with removal failures.

The first stage removes text input and cross-attention layers from a pretrained video generation model, motivated by the authors' observation that text conditioning is not best suited to this task. The second stage distills the remover using successful videos produced in the first stage. An inner maximization searches for adversarial input noise that causes failures, while an outer minimization trains the model to produce good removals under that challenging noise.

The resulting system achieves reported state-of-the-art removal results with as few as six sampling steps and without classifier-free guidance. Experiments support the effectiveness of both the approach and its performance against existing methods. The central finding is that explicitly training against failure-inducing noise can accompany a lighter architecture and shorter sampling process.
neurips-2025-minimax-remover-taming-bad-.tldr: MiniMax-Remover simplifies video diffusion and trains against failure-inducing noise to achieve strong object removal in as few as six steps.

paragraphs: This paper studies quantum algorithms for approximate correlated and coarse correlated equilibria in multiplayer general-sum games. These equilibrium concepts offer alternatives to Nash equilibrium, whose computation is PPAD-hard in general-sum games. The authors focus on normal-form games and measure how many queries the algorithms need as the numbers of players and actions increase.

For correlated equilibria, the approach introduces quantum improvements to a multiscale multiplicative weight update method. With approximation accuracy fixed, its query complexity scales as m times the square root of n, up to logarithmic factors, where m counts players and n counts actions. For coarse correlated equilibria, the authors extend techniques from quantum zero-sum game algorithms to the multiplayer setting.

The coarse-correlated algorithm has query complexity scaling as m times the square root of n divided by epsilon to the power 2.5, again up to logarithmic factors. Quantum query lower bounds show that both algorithms are nearly optimal in their dependence on player and action counts. This near-optimality claim concerns those dimensions and query complexity, rather than every aspect of computation.
neurips-2025-near-optimal-quantum-algori.tldr: Quantum algorithms compute approximate correlated equilibria with nearly optimal query scaling in the numbers of players and actions.

paragraphs: XDiff3D aims to improve how 3D semantic segmentation transfers across domains. The paper argues that methods centered on individual objects overlook useful relationships among objects. It draws on diffusion models' ability to represent varied object combinations and spatial arrangements, seeking to transfer that contextual information into 3D representations.

The framework first constructs object agent queries from diffusion features. These queries aggregate semantic information about individual instances and provide an interface for representing dependencies among objects. A separate component disentangles fine-grained local details from the queries so that those details do not interfere with the 3D semantic representation. Together, these components connect instance information with broader scene relationships.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks and task settings report state-of-the-art performance and support the effectiveness of the framework. The stated contribution is a way to use diffusion-derived context for cross-domain segmentation, rather than treating each object's appearance as the entire source of useful information. The results indicate that modeling semantic dependencies among objects can strengthen generalization in the evaluated 3D tasks.
neurips-2025-no-object-is-an-island-enha.tldr: XDiff3D transfers object relationships from diffusion features into 3D representations to improve cross-domain semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: FedWBA combines personalized federated learning with Bayesian uncertainty estimation for clients whose data distributions differ. The paper identifies two obstacles: local posterior estimates often use restrictive distribution families, and servers often combine them by simply averaging parameters. Its approach changes both how each client represents uncertainty and how the server aggregates those representations.

Clients use particle-based variational inference, representing their posterior through a collection of particles rather than a prescribed parametric form. The server combines these representations with a particle-based Wasserstein barycenter. This aggregation accounts for the geometry of the distributions being combined, making the global update more meaningful than naive parameter averaging in the proposed framework.

The theoretical analysis gives a per-iteration lower bound on the decrease in KL divergence for local inference. It also shows convergence of the global barycenter to the true parameter as client data size grows. Experiments report better prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and convergence rate than baselines, with ablations supporting robustness. The global convergence statement is an increasing-data result, distinct from the finite experimental comparisons.
neurips-2025-personalized-bayesian-feder.tldr: FedWBA uses particle-based client posteriors and Wasserstein aggregation to improve personalized federated prediction and uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: This paper addresses cryo-electron microscopy reconstruction when the observed molecules do not all have the same structure. Extremely noisy two-dimensional images must support an inferred three-dimensional model, while particles may bend or change shape and may sometimes lack particular parts. A useful reconstruction method must therefore accommodate both conformational flexibility and compositional variation.

The proposed framework represents the structure with a hierarchical Gaussian mixture model, drawing inspiration partly from Gaussian Splatting for changing scenes. Before reconstruction, it infers a segmentation of the particle into parts. That part-based organization supplies an inductive bias: the representation is structured around components that help it describe shape changes and differences in which components are present.

On complex experimental datasets, the framework reveals structures described as biologically meaningful. It also establishes a new state of the art on CryoBench, a benchmark for methods handling cryo-EM heterogeneity. These findings support combining part discovery with hierarchical representation when reconstructing variable molecular populations, rather than forcing their structural differences into a single undifferentiated model.
neurips-2025-reconstructing-heterogeneou.tldr: A part-based hierarchical Gaussian model reconstructs flexible and compositionally variable biomolecules, achieving state-of-the-art CryoBench results.

paragraphs: StreamForest addresses streaming video understanding when a model cannot retain all historical visual features. It combines a persistent memory of earlier events with detailed perception of the current scene. The architecture is designed around the need to preserve useful history while continuing to reason about incoming video under limited computational resources.

Its Persistent Event Memory Forest organizes frames into multiple trees representing events. Decisions about this organization use temporal distance, content similarity, and merge frequency. A Fine-grained Spatiotemporal Window separately captures detailed short-term cues. The paper also introduces OnlineIT for streaming-video instruction tuning and ODV-Bench for evaluation in autonomous-driving scenarios, extending the contribution beyond the memory architecture.

Reported accuracies are 77.3% on StreamingBench, 60.5% on OVBench, and 55.6% on OVO-Bench. With visual memory compressed to 1,024 tokens, the model retains 96.8% of its default-setting average accuracy across eight benchmarks. That last figure is a relative retention measure, showing how much evaluated performance survives compression. Together, the findings support the architecture's balance between long-term memory and current-scene detail.
neurips-2025-streamforest-efficient-onli.tldr: StreamForest combines event-organized memory with detailed short-term perception to understand streaming video under tight memory budgets.

paragraphs: This paper improves task planning for embodied agents that use language models to generate executable control code. Such code can fail when the model has incomplete or outdated information about the environment. The problem becomes particularly important in dynamic or partially observable settings, where a plausible plan may rely on observations the agent does not actually have.

The proposed framework combines explicit symbolic verification with interactive validation during code generation. During validation, it creates exploratory code that interacts with the environment to obtain missing observations while preserving states relevant to the task. This makes information gathering part of plan construction and helps connect generated instructions to the situation in which they will execute.

Evaluation covers RLBench and real-world dynamic, partially observable scenarios. The paper reports a 46.2% improvement in task success rates over Code as Policies baselines and more than 86.8% executability for task-relevant actions. These findings support integrating verification and observation gathering into code generation. They demonstrate improved reliability in the evaluated settings, rather than a guarantee that every generated plan will succeed.
neurips-2025-towards-reliable-code-as-po.tldr: Symbolic verification and interactive observation gathering make generated robot-control code more reliable in evaluated dynamic environments.

paragraphs: This paper develops uncertainty quantification for physics-informed neural networks using extended fiducial inference. It identifies a difficulty with Bayesian and dropout approaches: choosing a prior distribution or dropout rate that yields honest confidence sets requires additional information. The proposed method instead aims to construct such confidence sets from observed data.

The method uses a narrow-neck hyper-network to learn the parameters of the physics-informed network and quantify their uncertainty. Its uncertainty construction is based on imputed random errors in the observations. This connects the range of plausible network parameters to the observational-error mechanism within the extended fiducial framework, rather than requiring the prior or dropout-rate choice highlighted by the authors.

The paper claims rigorous confidence sets based solely on observations and presents a new theoretical framework extending extended fiducial inference to large-scale models. It also removes the need for sparse hyper-networks and reports improved automaticity and robustness of inference. The significance is a statistical route to assessing uncertainty alongside scientific predictions, with the authors positioning these guarantees as a foundation for more reliable and interpretable use of PINNs.
neurips-2025-uncertainty-quantification-.tldr: An extended fiducial method uses observational errors and a hyper-network to construct rigorous uncertainty sets for physics-informed neural networks.

paragraphs: VideoHallu tests whether video-understanding models notice events that violate physics or common sense. The paper argues that success on familiar real-world videos can leave open whether models understand visual evidence or rely on learned visual-language associations. It therefore adds negative-control examples containing physically impossible or logically inconsistent scenes.

The dataset uses synthetic videos generated with tools including Veo2, Sora, and Kling. Experts annotate question-answer pairs across four categories of violations designed to be straightforward for human reasoning. These examples test whether a model can recognize an inconsistency in what it sees, extending evaluation beyond ordinary scenes where familiar associations may produce plausible answers.

Several evaluated models, including Qwen-2.5-VL, Video-R1, and VideoChat-R1, hallucinate or miss violations despite strong results on real-world benchmarks. Reinforcement-learning post-training on the negative examples improves VideoHallu performance without degrading the standard-benchmark results reported. The findings expose weaknesses missed by conventional evaluations and provide evidence that targeted training can improve visual reasoning on these unusual scenes.
neurips-2025-videohallu-evaluating-and-m.tldr: VideoHallu exposes failures to recognize impossible video events and shows that targeted post-training can improve detection.

paragraphs: VITA-1.5 addresses the challenge of combining visual understanding with spoken conversation in one multimodal language model. Many such models emphasize images and text, while speech introduces a different kind of input and output. The paper focuses on developing strong capabilities in both areas so that vision and speech can participate in fluent interaction.

The authors use a carefully staged training process that progressively teaches the language model to understand visual and speech information. Their approach preserves strong vision-language capabilities while enabling speech-to-speech dialogue without separate automatic speech recognition and text-to-speech modules. Removing those separate modules from the interaction process significantly accelerates end-to-end multimodal responses, according to the paper.

Comparisons with state-of-the-art systems across image, video, and speech benchmarks show strong capabilities in both visual and spoken tasks. The findings support the training strategy as a way to combine these modalities within an interactive model. Although the title names GPT-4o as an ambition, the supplied results establish strong benchmark performance and faster responses without stating that full GPT-4o parity has been achieved.
neurips-2025-vita-1-5-towards-gpt-4o-lev.tldr: VITA-1.5 uses staged training to combine strong visual understanding with faster speech-to-speech interaction without separate ASR or TTS modules.
